draft.title: The classical bureaucratic approach
card: The classical bureaucratic approach manages a business through a clear structure and written rules. It draws on the ideas of Max Weber and Henri Fayol.
Authority comes from the top. A hierarchy is a chain of command, where each worker reports to one manager above them.
Each job has a set role, and written rules and procedures say how tasks are done. This makes work consistent and orderly.
The cost is that a business can become slow and rigid. A decision may need approval from several levels, and rules may not suit an unusual case.
draft.remember: Hierarchy, written rules and set roles bring order, but can make a business slow and rigid.

a.q: Which business is run mainly on the bureaucratic approach?
opts: Staff follow a written manual and report to one supervisor
Managers pay staff by the number of items each makes
Staff in each team choose their own roles and goals
Managers change their style to suit each new problem
a.why: A written manual and a single line of reporting show rules and a chain of command. Paying by output is a different approach, and the other two options leave out rules and hierarchy.
a.clue: Look for written rules and a chain of command.

b.q: Hana runs a council office in Bathurst. Every request needs a form signed by three levels of managers. Customers say it is slow, but errors are rare. What does this show?
opts: Order from rules, but slowness from a rigid structure
Speed from clear roles, but errors from weak rules
Better motivation from teamwork, but slow decisions
Fast decisions from the top, but too many errors
b.why: Signatures from several levels and written forms are features of a bureaucratic structure. They give order and few errors, but they slow decisions. Teamwork is not what the case describes.
b.clue: The case describes several approval levels and forms.

a.best: Staff follow a written manual and report to one supervisor

b.best: Order from rules, but slowness from a rigid structure
